Computing Consumer Tech Space & Aerospace Earnings Menu Money & Markets Economic Indicators Markets Personal Finance Earnings Menu Lifestyle Cars & Bikes Collecting Entertainment Food & Fine Dining Health and Fitness Real Estate Travel General Trivia 7 warning signs a home may face flood damage, from flood zones to cracked walls 
 Flood risk comes from where a house sits and how it is kept. Seven signs, from FEMA zones to cracked walls, show what to check.
 1 / 9 List slides 7 warning signs a home may face flood damage, from flood zones to cracked walls List slides Previous Start over By Cris Tolomia · Updated November 6, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Most people picture a flood as a disaster for river towns, something that happens to houses on the wrong side of a line on a map. In practice, the damage now reaches the basements of ordinary city homes by the thousands. At least 70,000 basements were flooded on Chicago's West Side and in its suburbs during a single storm in 2023, the Chicago Sun-Times reports , and in Ottawa more than 5,000 homes ended up with flooded basements after a July 1 storm, according to CBC News . Heavy storms are also becoming more common, though not at the same pace everywhere. Chicago has seen a sevenfold increase in the likelihood of a heavy storm over the past century, according to the Chicago Sun-Times . Across the U.S., severe flooding is increasing in certain regions, according to the CDC . For an owner, the useful question is not only whether a home sits inside a mapped zone. It is what about the house and the ground around it lets water in.
 Spotting the warning signs early matters because a flooded owner often pays alone. Flood damage generally falls outside what private insurers will pay for, according to the Chicago Sun-Times . "It's better to have the coverage and not need it than to need the coverage and not have it," Anne Marie Thomas, director of consumer and industry relations at the Insurance Bureau of Canada, told CBC News. An ordinary policy may leave a flooded owner with nothing, and the time to fix that gap is before a storm arrives. Many of the warning signs are visible well ahead of time: in the yard, on the basement walls, and in the equipment that keeps a basement dry. Checking the house early costs far less than discovering the risk through a flooded basement and a repair bill that no one else will pay.
 MitigateNow set out to identify the warning signs that a home faces flood damage risk, from the official flood map to an aging sump pump, a nearby creek, and a cracked basement wall. Some of those signs come with the address, and an owner cannot change them. Others come from the condition of the house, and an owner can find and fix them. The lesson across all of them is that flood risk changes with the weather and with upkeep, so a basement that stayed dry last year is no guarantee for the next storm.
 Designated flood zone 
 Illustration: Quartz
 An owner can check this sign without stepping inside the house, because it comes with the address. MitigateNow ranks a designated flood zone as the first warning sign of flood risk. On FEMA's official maps, location alone marks the risk, and that location affects both what an owner must insure and what the home is worth. A homeowner whose federally regulated mortgage covers a house inside the zone must carry flood insurance for the full term of the loan, according to the Federal Reserve Board . The owner pays that premium whether or not the house has ever taken on a drop of water, because lenders require the coverage for the designation and not for any actual flood. Every later buyer with that kind of mortgage takes on the same requirement, and buyers weigh the zone in what they will pay for the home as well as in its running costs.
 A house can end up inside the zone even though nothing about it has changed, because FEMA redraws the maps while the ground stays put. The Federal Reserve Board estimates that each lender sends about eight notices a year about flood coverage that lapsed because of remapping. For lenders, a gap in coverage caused by a new map is a routine matter, not a rare one. An owner who ignores such a notice still pays, because the lender can buy a policy and charge the borrower for it, and the owner ends up paying for coverage someone else chose. Holding a policy of one's own keeps that choice with the owner. Since 2019, lenders have had to accept private policies that meet the legal definition of flood insurance, which lets an owner compare options instead of waiting for the lender to pick one. The habit worth keeping is to check the flood map again each time FEMA redraws it, not only on the day of purchase.
 For all the money that depends on it, the zone is a regulatory line drawn on a map. "Floods do not stay inside the lines on a map," MitigateNow co-founder Raechel Iveson said. A home outside the zone can still flood, and no lender there requires flood coverage, so the decision about protection rests entirely on the owner.
 The map shows who has to pay, but only the condition of the house and the lot around it shows whether water is likely to get in.
 Poor drainage at the foundation 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Water that collects against a house is a flood risk that no map will flag. MitigateNow counts a badly drained lot, with water pooling at the foundation, among its warning signs, on the grounds that the way a property drains can put it at risk whatever its flood zone. An owner whose home sits safely outside the line on paper still has a question to answer. The answer is in the yard, in any puddle that lingers by the foundation hours after a storm has passed.
 The usual cause of that standing water is the slope of the ground. Raechel Iveson, author of the MitigateNow guide, says the way a lot is graded often lies behind these drainage problems. If the soil tips toward the walls instead of away, every rain carries water to the foundation rather than off the property. This is one of the few early signs an owner can correct, since a house can't be moved to a new address but the ground around it can be regraded. A dry summer lawn proves very little. The real test is where the water goes during and after a heavy rain.
 A yard that drains well does not rule out a flooded basement, because water can also rise through the floor drain from the city sewer below. "That's where you can get a backup from the mainline sewer up into your basement, and that's really nasty, and you don't want that," Kyle Chambers, division manager of sewer engineering for the City of London in Ontario, told CBC News. The concern therefore covers what happens once water reaches the house's own pipes, as well as where rain pools outside.
 Many owners in London have already sought help with that problem. The city approved more than 200 applications to its Basement Flooding Grant Program over two years, according to CBC News . An owner who watches the yard during a storm and knows how the basement drains connect learns more about the house than a flood map can show.
 Low-lying ground 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A house that sits below the street or at the bottom of a slope receives the rain that falls on the higher lots around it. MitigateNow counts elevation as a strong predictor of flooding, since runoff collects in low spots and basements there flood fast. A basement set below the surrounding ground has no lower place for that runoff to go. Low ground often shows its nature in its history. Chatham, a low-lying Chicago neighborhood that floods today, was known as Mud Lake in the mid- to late 1800s, according to the Chicago Sun-Times . Land that held water before anyone built on it tends to stay wet after the houses go up. The first thing an owner or buyer should inspect is the ground under the house, not only the house itself.
 Elevation sets up the risk, but the sewers around a house decide how often that risk becomes a flood. Low ground leaves little room for water, either in the soil or in the pipes. Raechel Iveson, a co-founder of MitigateNow, says that where the land offers no natural drainage, a modest shower can collect in its lowest spots. Chicago's sewers can take in 2 inches of rain over a day with little risk of flooding, but some storms there bring more than 8.5 inches in that span, according to the Chicago Sun-Times . On low lots, the water the sewers can't take collects in basements. The height of a lot alone can't tell an owner how safe it is, because the pipes that serve it matter as much.
 A low home tends to flood again and again, with each storm sending runoff back to the same places. "The most vulnerable communities are being hit now repetitively," Cyatharine Alias, urban resilience director at the Center for Neighborhood Technology, told the Chicago Sun-Times. Help from the city is uncertain and far off. A proposed tunnel for Chicago's Far Southeast Side is estimated to cost $1 billion and has no funding. Until a project like that is paid for and built, protecting a low-lying basement falls to the owner.
 A buyer looking at a house below street level should treat the risk as permanent and count protection as a lasting cost of owning that ground.
 Nearby waterways and storm drains 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A creek behind the house looks like scenery, and a storm drain at the curb looks like the thing that carries rain away. MitigateNow includes nearby water among its warning signs because a river can spill over its banks, a flash flood can strike, and a storm drain can back up once more rain reaches it than it can carry. The storm drain is the easiest of the three to overlook, because a house needs no river view to sit close to water. No set distance from a stream or drain makes a home safe. Risk generally rises closer to water, but the point where a home becomes too close depends on the local terrain and drainage and on the official flood zone, so an owner has to weigh the ground and the map together.
 The danger from nearby water that matters most is the sudden flood, not the slow rise that gives a family time to carry furniture upstairs. Flash floods cause among the highest number of flood deaths, according to the CDC . A stream or drain close to a house is one way a flash flood can reach it. Across the U.S., flooding of all kinds kills about 98 people a year, mostly by drowning, which makes it a threat to the people in a house as well as to its carpets and drywall. For a household next to a creek or a low-lying drain, the useful question becomes how quickly the family could get out, not only what the water might ruin.
 A dry spell offers no reassurance. A creek that has barely trickled for months is easy to forget, but drought conditions may make flash floods more likely, according to the CDC . A quiet stream next door may carry no less risk after a dry season, and possibly more.
 Water near a house should be judged by what it could do in an hour of hard rain, not by how it looks on a dry afternoon.
 Water stains and mold 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A tide line on a basement wall or a musty smell in one corner shows that water has already come into the house. MitigateNow says that water getting in during ordinary rain suggests heavier storms will do worse. Mold also needs moisture to grow, and the CDC says that the moisture can come from leaks as well as from flooding. A stain proves that water is reaching the wall. It doesn't prove that the water comes from the ground. A leaking pipe, window or roof can leave the same mark. The owner's first job is to trace the water to its source, since a dripping pipe and seeping groundwater need very different repairs.
 A lab test for mold gives an owner little to act on. The CDC advises against testing for mold, and no official limit exists for how much mold is too much indoors. The useful record is the damage anyone can see. An owner who photographs the stains before any cleanup has a record that may help a restoration crew decide which repairs the basement needs. The pictures also show a contractor how far the water reached. A visible stain is enough reason to start repairs.
 Dampness also affects the air a household breathes. A 2004 review by the Institute of Medicine found evidence linking indoor mold to coughing and wheezing, according to the CDC . Scrubbing the wall clean does not solve the problem while the wall stays wet. "If mold is growing in your home, you need to clean up the mold and fix the moisture problem," the CDC said. When the dampness comes from humid air rather than a leak, the owner has a clear limit to aim for. The CDC sets that limit at 50% indoor humidity, and an inexpensive meter tells an owner whether the basement stays under it.
 Caught early, a stain costs little to investigate, while the wet wall behind it costs more the longer it stays wet.
 Aging sump pumps 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Most owners think about the sump pump, the machine whose only job is to send groundwater back outside, only after it has already stopped. MitigateNow warns that pumps can fail without warning and let groundwater flood a basement quickly. Once the pump stops, nothing else keeps the rising water out, and the owner gets no slow drip to notice and no time to react. "Pumps do not last forever, and they can quit without much warning," said Raechel Iveson, a co-founder, advisor and board member at MitigateNow. The sign to look for is not only a pump that sounds tired but a pump that nothing would replace if it stopped.
 Replacing an old pump solves only part of the problem, because a pump in perfect working order still stops when the power does. In 2023, about 300,000 U.S. households reported flooded basements or crawlspaces after their sump pumps lost power, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . A new pump alone does not make a home safe. Power outages are common for any pump that runs on grid power, and 33.9 million U.S. households lost electricity over the same 12 months. The damage comes when the power fails while water is collecting in the pit, at the moment the household needs the pump most. Battery or generator backup belongs to this sign, and a pump without backup is inadequate however new it is.
 Owners in some places need that backup more urgently, because the power goes out there far more often. In Detroit, 44.8 percent of households reported an outage in a year, the highest share among the country's largest metro areas, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . An owner there who relies on a pump with no backup faces that risk often. The checklist has two lines: how old the pump is, and what keeps it running when the lights go out.
 Cracked foundation walls 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Many owners treat a hairline crack in a basement wall as normal aging, something to paint over and forget. MitigateNow lists a damaged foundation or basement wall among its warning signs because water pressing against the outside of a cracked wall has an open route indoors. When the ground around a house is saturated, water under pressure can move through those openings. An insurer in Ottawa blamed one homeowner's flooded basement on hydrostatic pressure through visible foundation cracks, according to CBC News . Any crack in a basement wall is a likely place for water to enter the next time the soil is soaked.
 Once water is inside, the route it took can decide who pays for the damage. Insurers treat water that rises into a basement through its floor and foundation as groundwater flooding, according to CBC News , and some policies leave that kind of water out. The Ottawa homeowner's policy excluded groundwater flooding, and the insurer denied the claim. An owner with a cracked wall can end up uninsured as well as flooded, and checking the walls and checking the policy belong on the same weekend's to-do list.
 Sealing a crack from inside the basement does not fix it for good. "The only permanent solution is to address the problem at the source, which is at the exterior of the foundation," Alex Berezowski of The Foundation Experts told CBC News. An owner who takes on that outside repair should expect to excavate around the house and spend $20,000 or more, which makes it a construction project rather than a handyman job.
 An owner who finds the crack while the basement is still dry can plan that repair and review the policy before the next storm, instead of facing both at once.
